title: Bengal plans to let industry hold more land in proportion to investment, easing ceiling law
dek: A Land Reforms (Third Amendment) Bill expected in the winter session would change Section 14Y, which caps company landholdings at about 24 acres without state clearance. Officials say the ceiling stays and there will be no forced acquisition.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
West Bengal's government is preparing to relax the limits on how much land companies can hold, letting larger investors keep proportionally more land, in a bid to attract big factories to a state where land for industry has long been politically explosive, according to reports.

The West Bengal Land Reforms (Third Amendment) Bill, 2026, is expected to be tabled in the Assembly's winter session. It would change Section 14Y of the West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955, the clause under which the state permits companies to hold land above the ceiling, according to reports citing officials. The size of the holding allowed would depend on the size of the investment and the type of project.

## What would change

Under the current law, a company or organisation cannot directly buy more than 75 bighas, about 24 acres, of non-urban land; larger purchases need state government clearance under Section 14Y. That limit has long been cited by industry as a major obstacle to putting together large plots for manufacturing and infrastructure, reports said. A notification issued in July 2024 already allows land above the ceiling for industrial parks or estates, financial hubs and townships.

The new framework would scale permitted holdings to investment, subject to scrutiny and conditions, with safeguards against hoarding, diversion of land to other uses and speculative holding, according to reports. It is meant to work alongside a GIS-based inventory of industrial land and a transparent, time-bound allocation system. One report last week said a new standard operating procedure for allocating industrial land could follow in January.

Chief Secretary Manoj Agarwal and Subrata Gupta, chief adviser to Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, had earlier indicated the proposal, reports said. An official quoted anonymously in reports said the ceiling system would not be dismantled, that industrial growth would not come at farmers' expense and that there would be no forcible acquisition. The Bill has not yet been published, so its final wording may differ.

## Background

The plan follows the Investment Promotion Policy, 2026, which Adhikari unveiled on 5 November. Under it, the state will buy land from willing owners for a land bank, pool plots with farmers' participation and use the 2013 central land acquisition law, but will not take land by force. At an industry event on Tuesday, Adhikari again set out that approach of buying and pooling land, according to reports.

Land has shaped Bengal's politics for two decades. Protests against acquisition for the Tata Nano factory at Singur and a proposed chemical hub at Nandigram in 2006-07 helped bring down the Left Front government in 2011. The Trinamool Congress government that followed largely kept the state out of land purchase for industry, which business groups said held back large projects.

## What happens next

The Bill is expected in the Assembly's winter session; the Assembly is also due to vote on renaming the state Paschim Banga on 9 December. No response from opposition parties to the proposed amendment had been reported by Thursday. Changes to land-reform law in Bengal have historically drawn close scrutiny from farmers' groups and the Left, and the debate is likely to turn on the safeguards the government writes into the final text.
